item.title: Police and ODPP say 2.64 tonnes of cocaine in Vatia Wharf bust secure, destruction application on 15th Oct
item.description: As questions arise on whether the 2.64 tonnes of cocaine from the Vatia Wharf bust with an estimated street value of around $3 billion is still intact without being tampered with, both the Police and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions say the drug exhibit remains in Police custody in a secure location. item.content:encoded:
As questions arise on whether the 2.64 tonnes of cocaine from the Vatia Wharf bust with an estimated street value of around $3 billion is still intact without being tampered with, both the Police and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions say the drug exhibit remains in Police custody in a secure location.

While answering questions from fijivillage News, the Office of the DPP says t he cocaine seized in the Vatia case in January this year remains in police custody under the supervision of the Director CID, with 24 hour security and surveillance measures in place.

When asked on whether the cocaine in this case will be retested based on the $50 million worth of cocaine going missing from the Suva High Court Exhibit Room for the John Nikolic and Joshua Aziz Rahman drug cases, the ODPP says the drugs from Vatia have already been tested, with the results returning positive for cocaine.

They say further testing and weighing may be ordered by the Court as part of the destruction order.

The Office of the DPP also clarifies that the State raised its intention to seek the destruction of the drugs at an early stage of the proceedings.

They say since then, the matter has progressed through the necessary pre-trial processes, including the confirmation of counsel, consolidation of charges and fixing of a hearing date.

These processes also provide the defence with an opportunity, if they wish, to arrange further testing at their own cost before the drugs are destroyed.

The Office of the DPP is now progressing the necessary application for destruction, which is scheduled to be made in court on the 15 th of this month.

We are also asking about other drug exhibits following the missing drugs from the Suva High Court Exhibit Room.

The ODPP says from their end, they are unaware of any other cases where drugs that initially tested positive have subsequently returned a negative result on re-testing.

They say as the Commissioner of Police has indicated, a full audit of drug exhibits in their custody will be conducted to establish the position across other cases.

The ODPP says it recognises the importance of the proper and timely management of drug exhibits, particularly given the risks associated with their continued storage.

The ODPP will continue to prioritise the destruction of drug exhibits where they are no longer required for evidential purposes and the necessary legal requirements have been satisfied.

We have also asked Chief Justice Salesi Temo and Chief Registrar Tomasi Bainivalu on whether they will conduct a full audit of all the court exhibits, and test the drug exhibits. They have not responded.

item.title: Manumanunitoga backs moderate chastisement as corrective measure for children in Constitution Bill
item.description: The issue of moderate chastisement of children as a corrective measure should be considered separately from corporal punishment. Fijian Teachers’ Association General Secretary Paula Manumanunitoga says there was wide consultation on the issue by the Constitution Review Commission.
item.content:encoded:
The issue of moderate chastisement of children as a corrective measure should be considered separately from corporal punishment.

Fijian Teachers’ Association General Secretary Paula Manumanunitoga says there was wide consultation on the issue by the Constitution Review Commission.

He claims 95 percent of indigenous Fijians supported the provision in the Constitution Amendment Bill allowing moderate chastisement to correct children’s misbehaviour.

Manumanunitoga says the provision was later shelved because of concerns relating to the United Nations and funding.

He says Fiji should not compromise its values because of foreign funding or outside influence.

Manumanunitoga also says changing what he considers to be God’s law could have serious consequences for the country.

item.title: Students Associations raise concern on child chastisement provision in the Constitution Bill
item.description: Student Association representatives from theÂ University of the South Pacific andÂ the University of Fiji have raised concerns over the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill that has a section on moderate chastisement of children for the purposes of correction. They say while parents and teachers have a responsibility to guide children and maintain discipline, any form of physical punishment must
item.content:encoded:
Student Association representatives from theÂ University of the South Pacific andÂ the University of Fiji have raised concerns over the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill that has a section on moderate chastisement of children for the purposes of correction.

They say while parents and teachers have a responsibility to guide children and maintain discipline, any form of physical punishment must be carefully considered because of its possible effects on children's confidence, learning and well-being.

University of the South Pacific Students Association President Adi Cama says the proposed amendment needs to be considered carefully, particularly the meaning and application of the term â€œmoderate chastisement”.

Cama says parents and teachers have a responsibility to guide and correct children, but discipline should respect the dignity, safety and wellbeing of the child.

USPSA says if the amendment becomes law, there should be clear definitions, safeguards and proper guidance for parents and teachers.

The University of Fiji Students Association President Rodney Vakaloloma also says he does not support physical violence against children as a form of correction or discipline.

Vakaloloma says the student perspective should also be considered through documents such as the Law 205 Constitution and the Constitution draft prepared by students.

He has advised people to refer to the student Constitution draft, which raises and reflects the views of students on constitutional matters.

Meanwhile a medical student who wishes to remain anonymous says that he does not support physical punishment, saying there are other measures that can be used to maintain discipline among children.

The student also raised concerns about the possible impact of physical punishment on students' schoolwork, confidence and participation in the classroom.

He says children could become afraid to ask questions or speak openly in the classroom if they fear being physically punished.

The students associations' representatives say the views of students and young people should be considered as discussions continue on the proposed constitution amendments.

item.title: Vanuabalavu Day focuses on community development, investment and cultural preservation
item.description: Raising funds for community development and investment in Vanuabalavu, while preserving culture and strengthening relationships, will be the key focus of this year’s Vanuabalavu Day, which will be held from tomorrow until Friday. Speaking at a press conference on the joint venture in copra investment with Waitavoro Enterprise, Vanuabalavu Vision Limited Secretary Tomi Waqa Finau says part of the d
item.content:encoded:
Raising funds for community development and investment in Vanuabalavu, while preserving culture and strengthening relationships, will be the key focus of this year’s Vanuabalavu Day, which will be held from tomorrow until Friday.

Speaking at a press conference on the joint venture in copra investment with Waitavoro Enterprise, Vanuabalavu Vision Limited Secretary Tomi Waqa Finau says part of the development plans for communities on the island includes rebuilding their church, which has been in the planning phase for the past two years.

He says people attending Vanuabalavu Day will also have the opportunity to experience signature Lauan dishes such as vakasakera and spit-roast pork.

He adds that this is the sixth year the festival has been held.

Vanuabalavu Day starts tomorrow at 9am at the Fiji Sports Council car park.
